In line with #AI authored projects > Formalized statement of the Weil conjectures? :
I have auto-formalized some solutions to Erdős problems. I was looking into which solutions to Erdős problems might be the hardest to formalize unconditionally, and I think there's one whose solution currently goes via the classification of finite simple groups (CFSG).

For now, it may be worthwhile to formalize the conditional implication. Accordingly, I am curious: is there a Lean 4 statement of the classification available anywhere?
Not a public one as far as I know. The statement would be a lot of work but who knows these days.
The "proper" definitions involve taking fixed points on algebraic subgroups which is still beyond the reach of mathlib. Certainly you could write down hacky definitions with less difficulty.
I found this (incomplete) statement from Lean 3 days: https://github.com/formalabstracts/formalabstracts/blob/b0173da1af45421239d44492eeecd54bf65ee0f6/src/group_theory/classification.lean#L48-L55

Thomas Browning said:

The "proper" definitions involve taking fixed points on algebraic subgroups which is still beyond the reach of mathlib.

Can you say more about what you mean here?

The finite groups of Lie type can be defined by taking various semisimple algebraic groups GGG over finite fields FFF and taking the fixed points of some automorphism of G(F‾)G(\overline{F})G(F). For instance, see here: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ree_group#Construction
(At least, that's my rough understanding, although I've never looked into it too carefully)

I don't know if it is good for formalizing, but there is an alternative way to describe the Suzuki and Ree series using algebraic groups over twisted rings, where twisted rings are commutative rings of characteristic p equipped with a distinguished square root of Frobenius. This is a discovery of Naert in his dissertation this paper has a summary. Aside from these families, the other groups of Lie type (except the Tits group) are given by rational points of algebraic groups over finite fields.

There's a lot of leeway in what might considered a "statement of CFSG." For example, for the Monster, you could take a minimalist approach and just say something along the lines of, "there exists a finite simple group of this order". But that's probably not going to be enough to derive the consequences that people infer from CFSG; you'll probably need to at least specify some of the properties of the Monster.

That is an excellent point. For example, the positive resolution of Schreier’s conjecture (outer automorphism groups of finite simple groups are solvable) is often cited as a consequence of the classification, but if you want to use it in your work, you need more than the bare claim, “this list is complete.” Someone has to compute all of the outer automorphism groups.

For the sporadics I was envisioning just giving a presentation (and not even proving that the presented group was finite), which seemed like a manageable thing to do (I think the monster has one with something like 12 generators and 50-or-so relations which can be written algorithmically)

I saw one suggestion to state this:

the twenty-six sporadic groups exist, and each of them (except M11M_{11}M11​) is uniquely determined up to isomorphism as the only simple group with its centralizer of involution pattern.

I've just put up TauCetiRoadmap#156, a roadmap to get to the statement of CFSG in Tau Ceti. I think this one should not take too long.

Would anyone be interested in reviewing? If we can get this in, then the usual recipe:

uv tool install --force git+https://github.com/kim-em/TauCetiWorker.git
tauceti work --loop --roadmap-only CFSGStatement

will start generating PRs (and fixing/responding to review) to complete the roadmap. (See the README and zulip thread for more on the tauceti client.)

Kevin Buzzard said:

For the sporadics I was envisioning just giving a presentation (and not even proving that the presented group was finite), which seemed like a manageable thing to do (I think the monster has one with something like 12 generators and 50-or-so relations which can be written algorithmically)

I've just found this repo where some of the sporadic groups are defined and properties like order and simplicity are proven.

If you want to set it as a benchmark for computers you can use the Schreier conjecture as a proxy. I thought I was clever for thinking of this until I saw Kim Morrison had already posted it to Lean Eval :) https://lean-lang.org/eval/problems/schreier_conjecture/

What's nice about the conjecture is that it is easy to state and the only known proof requires the CFSG. I've been working on trying to formalize the Suzuki groups as an exercise, and now I know why people avoid explicit matrices in lean like the plague.

@Kim Morrison Regarding Schreier's conjecture, one can simplify the problem statement at https://lean-lang.org/eval/problems/schreier_conjecture/ further by dropping the non-abelian hypothesis.
The non-abelian hypothesis is sometimes used to state the conjecture slightly differently, but the form on the Lean eval page is the one that works for everything, which I have verified by actually proving the abelian case in Lean.

Boris Alexeev said:

Thomas Browning said:

The "proper" definitions involve taking fixed points on algebraic subgroups which is still beyond the reach of mathlib.

Can you say more about what you mean here?

There are at least three ways to define them: (1) fixed points of the Steinberg endomorphism on algebraic groups, (2) via simple Lie algebras, (3) subquotients of stabilizers of bilinear forms. I think (2) and (3) are somehow "ad hoc" and (1) provides a uniform construction.

As far as I know, all the three approaches are necessary for the proof of CFSG, and at some point one needs to show they are all equivalent.
(1), fixed points of Steinerg, is the approach in TauCetiRoadmap#156
